dct_description_sm: This data set on military activities in Cambridge Bay, Nunavut, since 1940, is being developed as part of a broader community-based history project -- a collaboration between a university-based historian and student researchers, the Kitikmeot Heritage Society, and other community organizations  exploring local experiences and definitions of community in Cambridge Bay and surrounding areas of the Kitikmeot region of Nunavut from 1930-80.  Drawing upon the oral histories of Inuit elders, archival materials in Ottawa and Yellowknife, and the expertise of the Kitikmeot Heritage Society and southern academics, we hope to develop innovative ways to co-create knowledge which enhances our understandings of the evolution of the Cambridge Bay community in the twentieth century.  We anticipate that this study will focus on issues related to the urbanization and settlement life of the Inuit, including socio-economic development, culture and language, health, harvesting activities, and the trans-generational transfer of knowledge. Our main goal is to reconcile different traditions of knowing to produce a more democratic history of the Kitikmeot region, to better educate Canadians (northern and southern), and to stimulate more cultural, social and political empowerment amongst Nunavummiut living in the Kitikmeot region.  Specific objectives include: . (re)writing/narrating the history of modern Arctic settlement/ colonization/ contact using the multiple perspectives of local inhabitants and experiential accounts . developing more culturally appropriate and democratic means to review, teach and understand the dynamics of Arctic and Inuit history . developing a participatory living history curriculum at the high school level which integrates textbook learning and skills to record history (such as video, audio, and archives) . creating an oral history bank/recording program through the Kitikmeot Heritage Society in Cambridge Bay. By focusing on the Kitikmeot region, and bringing contemporary reports, archival materials, and photographs into dialogue with Inuit Elders, we seek to produce a community history program in which Inuit see themselves and, through their oral histories, inform the broader academic debates about Northern Aboriginal community development in the twentieth century.
